intro: This unit follows one secret criminal society, the Sicilian Mafia, from the lemon groves around Palermo in the 1860s to courtrooms in Palermo and Chicago. The story reaches into our own time. You will meet the people who studied it, the people who feared it and the people who stood up to it. You will also meet Chinese American tongs and the triads, and see how their story differs.

The Mafia's strongest shield was omertà, a rule of silence. For more than a century it kept witnesses quiet and crimes unpunished. This unit is about how that silence was broken: by police reports, Senate hearings, new laws, brave insiders, judges who paid with their lives and ordinary neighbors acting together. Remember too that almost all Italian Americans and Chinese Americans had nothing to do with these groups, and many were their victims.

By the end, you will be able to explain where the Mafia came from and how it spread. You will be able to describe how the RICO Act and the Maxi Trial worked. You will also be able to weigh an insider's testimony, and to explain the real cost of organized crime to ordinary people.
bigQuestion: How did people break the Mafia's rule of silence, and what did it cost them?

title: The Mafia on Trial

chapters.title: From Sicily to America
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a secret society born in the citrus groves of Sicily become something the whole United States argued about?

story.title: Hands on the Screen
story.kicker: In March 1951, millions of Americans stop what they are doing to watch a Senate hearing on live television.
paragraphs: It is March 1951 in New York City. In a crowded federal courtroom, a committee of United States senators is asking questions about organized crime. Bright lights hang over the tables. Television cameras stand in the room. Across the country, people gather around small black-and-white sets at home, in bars and in store windows to watch.

The witness at the table is Frank Costello, a gambling boss the newspapers call powerful. He does not want his face shown on camera. So the camera crew points at something else: his hands. Viewers watch his fingers move on the table while he answers, dodges or refuses to answer the senators' questions.

The man leading the hearings is Senator Estes Kefauver of Tennessee. Since May 1950, his committee has held hearings in about 14 cities, including Chicago. It has heard more than 600 witnesses. The Senate's own history office estimates that about 30 million Americans tuned in to the New York hearings that month.

For many viewers, this is the first time they have seen the people behind the headlines. The hearings raise a question Americans will argue about for decades. Is organized crime a set of local gangs? Or is it one secret society, with rules, a name and a reach across the whole nation?
story.think: Why might seeing only a witness's hands on television make viewers more curious, not less? What can a live hearing show that a newspaper story cannot?

lessons.title: Protection in the Lemon Groves
lessons.mainIdea: The Sicilian Mafia grew in western Sicily after 1860 by selling violent protection where the new Italian state was weak.
reading: In 1860, Giuseppe Garibaldi's volunteers landed in Sicily. Soon the island joined the new Kingdom of Italy. The new government was far away in the north. It had few police in the countryside and little trust from the people. Around Palermo, in the west of the island, rich lemon and orange groves earned good money. Anyone who could guard that wealth, or threaten it, had power.

In this setting, armed men began to sell *protection*. A landowner paid them to keep thieves away from his trees and his water. But the same men could also send the thieves. Paying was safer than refusing. A deal where people pay a group so the group will not harm them is called a *protection racket*. It grew strongest where the state was weakest.

The name came into use in these same years. A popular play set in Palermo's prison, I mafiusi di la Vicaria, was first staged in 1863. It made the word *mafioso* familiar to many people. In 1865 a government official in Palermo, Filippo Antonio Gualterio, used the word 'maffia' in a report to his superiors. Historians usually call this the first official use.

Historians such as Salvatore Lupo and John Dickie place the Mafia's beginnings in these decades, not in the Middle Ages. A popular legend says the Mafia began in 1282, or that its name is a secret code made of first letters. No record from that time supports either story. They are legends told much later.

a deal where people pay a group so the group will not harm them or their property
a member of the Mafia; the word became common in Sicily in the 1860s

lessons.title: Franchetti's Inquiry
lessons.mainIdea: In 1876 Leopoldo Franchetti studied Sicily on his own, and his 1877 report argued that violence there had become a business.
reading: In 1876, two young men from Tuscany, Leopoldo Franchetti and Sidney Sonnino, traveled through Sicily. No one sent them. They paid their own way and asked their own questions. They wanted to understand why the island was so violent. They also wanted to know why the new national government seemed unable to stop it.

They published what they found in 1877, in two volumes called La Sicilia nel 1876. Sonnino wrote about the hard lives of peasant farmers. Franchetti wrote about politics and government. A careful study of a problem, built on interviews and evidence, is called an *inquiry*. The Italian parliament held its own official inquiry into Sicily in those same years.

Franchetti's main idea was striking. He described what he called an *industry of violence*. In his view, violence in western Sicily was not wild or random. It was a service that some people bought and others sold, much like any trade. Landowners, estate managers and armed guards all took part in this market.

Many historians today build on Franchetti's idea. Diego Gambetta's 1993 book The Sicilian Mafia describes the Mafia as a business in private protection. Other historians, such as Salvatore Lupo and Letizia Paoli, add that it is also a *brotherhood*, with rituals, loyalty and political ties. Both views use the same evidence. They stress different parts of it.

words.d: a careful study of a problem, built on interviews and evidence

lessons.title: The Sangiorgi Report
lessons.mainIdea: From 1898 to 1900, Palermo's police chief Ermanno Sangiorgi mapped Mafia groups in detail, showing they were organized long before later trials.
reading: Ermanno Sangiorgi was the *questore*, the chief of police, of Palermo in the late 1890s. From November 1898 to February 1900 he sent 31 reports to the government in Rome. Together they run to about 485 pages. They describe the Mafia around Palermo in more detail than anyone had put on paper before.

Sangiorgi described eight Mafia groups. Sicilians called these groups *cosche*; one group is a cosca. Each group had its own territory in the citrus gardens around the city. He named and profiled 218 men. He wrote about their rules, their leaders and the ceremony that brought in new members.

For about a century, the report sat almost forgotten in the state archives in Rome. The historian Salvatore Lupo published it in full in 2011. The historian John Dickie described it for English readers. It matters because it shows that the Mafia's groups, rules and ritual already existed in the 1890s.

Sangiorgi's work did not end the Mafia. Police knowledge alone was not enough when witnesses stayed silent and powerful friends protected suspects. But his report is a *primary source*, a record made at the time by someone involved. Historians can compare it with what later witnesses said, and they find the same kind of structure.

lessons.title: Omertà, the Rule of Silence
lessons.mainIdea: Omertà is the rule of silence toward police and courts, and fear of breaking it let Mafia crimes go unpunished for generations.
reading: On 1 February 1893, Emanuele Notarbartolo was stabbed to death on a train near Palermo. He was a former mayor of the city. He had also run the Bank of Sicily and tried to clean up its dealings. Suspicion fell on a powerful member of parliament, Raffaele Palizzolo.

The case dragged through courts in Milan, Bologna and Florence. In 1902 a court in Bologna convicted Palizzolo, but a higher court threw out that verdict. In 1904 a court in Florence acquitted him for lack of evidence. Through all of it, Notarbartolo's son Leopoldo kept pushing for justice, while many witnesses said little or nothing.

That silence has a name: *omertà*. It is the Mafia's rule that members, and people around them, never help the police or the courts. Breaking it could bring punishment or death. Many ordinary people stayed silent, not out of loyalty, but out of fear. A crime with no witness willing to *testify* is very hard to prove in court.

This is why omertà runs through every part of this unit. The state could not win while people stayed quiet. Every real victory came when someone chose to speak, and when others protected them. Watch for that pattern in each story that follows, in Sicily and in America.

words.d: the Mafia's rule of silence: never help the police or the courts

to give evidence in court under oath

lessons.title: Leaving Sicily
lessons.mainIdea: Millions of Italians came to America to work; a small number of criminals followed and preyed mostly on other immigrants.
reading: Between about 1880 and 1920, about four million Italians moved to the United States. Most came from southern Italy and Sicily, and many were poor farmers. Sonnino's 1877 study had described how hard life was for Sicilian peasants. In America they built railroads, worked in factories, opened shops and raised families in cities like New York and Chicago.

Almost all of these *immigrants* had nothing to do with crime. But a small number of criminals came too, or grew up in the new neighborhoods. From about 1903 to 1915, some sent threatening letters signed with a black hand. They demanded money and threatened harm. Getting money by threats is called *extortion*. Police at the time said the Black Hand was a method used by many small gangs, not one society.

Most victims of the Black Hand were Italian immigrants themselves, and many fought back. In Chicago in November 1907, Italian Americans proposed a group called the White Hand Society. By early 1908 it had an office in the Masonic Temple building downtown. It offered rewards and pressed the police to act.

Prejudice made life harder. In New Orleans in 1891, after a trial ended without convictions in the murder of the police chief, a mob killed 11 Italian men. In 2019, the mayor of New Orleans formally apologized to Italian Americans. A *stereotype*, a fixed and unfair idea about a whole group, can do real harm.

lessons.title: The First American Families
lessons.mainIdea: Prohibition made gangs rich, and by the 1930s crime families built on the Sicilian pattern ran rackets in several American cities.
reading: On 16 January 1920, national *Prohibition* began. Making and selling alcohol was now against federal law. But millions of people still wanted to drink. Gangs of many backgrounds, including Irish, Jewish and Italian gangs, made fortunes supplying them. In Chicago, Johnny Torrio and then Al Capone built a large organization that later came to be called the Outfit.

Some of these gangs were organized like the Sicilian cosche. Each *crime family* had a boss, other leaders and members who swore loyalty in a ceremony. In the early 1930s, after a violent struggle among New York bosses, leaders set up a system of families with a council to settle disputes. New York came to have five families. Chicago had one main group, the Outfit.

The families lasted after Prohibition ended in 1933. They moved into gambling, loan-sharking, labor unions and other *rackets*, illegal businesses built on fraud or threats. Their power depended on bribing officials and on silence. For years, many officials said little about them. Some doubted a national organization existed. Others were paid not to look.

Remember what the families were not. They were never 'the Italians.' Only a very small share of Italian Americans ever took part. Many Italian Americans became police officers, prosecutors, judges and reporters who fought organized crime. Historians also stress that gangs of many backgrounds ran rackets in these years.

lessons.title: The Kefauver Committee
lessons.mainIdea: From 1950 to 1951, a Senate committee led by Estes Kefauver held hearings in about 14 cities, including Chicago, and put organized crime in the spotlight.
reading: In May 1950, the United States Senate formed a *special committee* to investigate organized crime that crossed state lines. A special committee is a group of senators set up for one task and for a limited time. Its chair was Estes Kefauver, a senator from Tennessee. Over the next year it held hearings in about 14 cities and heard more than 600 witnesses.

Chicago was one of those cities. Some Chicago testimony was taken in *closed session*, meaning the public and the press were kept out. One witness was a police captain, Daniel 'Tubbo' Gilbert, who was running for Cook County sheriff. He was asked how he had become so wealthy. His private testimony leaked to the press before the November 1950 election, and he lost.

The hearings also showed the danger to people who spoke up. On 25 September 1950, a former Chicago police lieutenant, William Drury, was shot and killed in Chicago. He had been expected to help the committee. His murder reminded everyone why so many witnesses were afraid to talk.

The committee held a *hearing*, not a trial. Senators could question witnesses under oath and publish what they learned. They could not convict anyone of a crime. But hearings can change what the public knows. That can push police, prosecutors and voters to act.

a meeting or hearing where the public and the press are kept out
a meeting where officials question witnesses under oath; it is not a trial

lessons.title: Crime on Live Television
lessons.mainIdea: Live TV in March 1951 reached millions, and the committee's report claimed a nationwide Mafia, a claim historians still debate.
reading: In March 1951 the committee held hearings in New York, and they were shown live on television. The Senate Historical Office estimates that about 30 million Americans watched. Frank Costello, a New York gambling boss, did not want his face shown. So the cameras showed his hands instead. Many viewers remembered those hands for years.

On 1 May 1951 the committee issued its Third Interim Report, an *interim report* meant to share results before the final one. It said there was a nationwide crime *syndicate*, a group of criminals working together, known as the Mafia. It said the Mafia had members in many large cities and controlled some of the most profitable rackets. It said the Mafia's power rested on force and murder.

Not everyone agreed. The scholar Joseph Albini in 1971, and Dwight C. Smith in The Mafia Mystique in 1975, argued that the evidence was thin. They said the committee relied too much on rumor and focused too much on one ethnic group. Later evidence confirmed that Italian American crime families existed and worked together. It did not show that one Mafia ran all organized crime in America.

This debate is a good lesson in evidence. A committee's *finding*, its stated conclusion, can be partly right and partly overstated. Historians test each part. Which claim has sworn testimony behind it? Which rests on police opinion? Which was later proved in court?

a group of people or businesses working together; here, criminals working together
the conclusion that a committee or court states after looking at evidence

lessons.title: A Trooper's Hunch at Apalachin
lessons.mainIdea: In November 1957, a state police sergeant's roadblock at Apalachin, New York, exposed a meeting of crime leaders from many states.
reading: Edgar Croswell was a sergeant in the New York State Police. He worked near Apalachin, a small town in upstate New York. He knew that Joseph Barbara, who owned a country estate there, had a criminal past. In November 1957 Croswell noticed signs that many out-of-town visitors were coming to Barbara's estate. He decided to watch.

On 14 November 1957, Croswell and other officers set up a *roadblock* near the estate. When the guests learned that police were outside, many tried to leave by car or ran into the woods. Officers stopped and identified 58 men from many states. Many were known leaders of crime families. Sam Giancana, a leader of Chicago's Outfit, is said to have escaped through the woods.

The police could not easily prove a crime. The men gave innocent-sounding reasons for being there. Some were later convicted of *conspiracy* for lying about why they met. But in 1960 a federal appeals court overturned those convictions in United States v. Bufalino. Simply being at a meeting is not, by itself, a crime.

Still, Apalachin changed minds. Before it, the FBI under J. Edgar Hoover had given organized crime little attention. Right after it, the FBI began its Top Hoodlum Program to gather *intelligence*, meaning organized information, on crime leaders. One observant officer had shown that the families were in contact across the country.

lessons.title: Valachi Names Cosa Nostra

reading: Joseph Valachi was a low-ranking member of a New York crime family. By the early 1960s he was in federal prison. He came to believe his own boss wanted him dead, and he agreed to talk to the government. It was a rare break in omertà by a sworn member in the United States.

In September and October 1963, the Senate's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations held public hearings. A *subcommittee* is a smaller group inside a larger committee. Its chair was Senator John McClellan of Arkansas. The hearings opened on 25 September, and Valachi first appeared before the cameras on 27 September. He testified on five days. Millions watched a sworn member describe the secret society from the inside.

Valachi said members called their organization *Cosa Nostra*, Italian for 'our thing.' He described an initiation ceremony, ranks such as boss and soldier, and the five New York families. He named many members. Most Americans had never heard the name before. Newspapers soon spread it everywhere.

Valachi's testimony had limits. He was a low-level member, so he saw only part of the organization. Some of his dates and details did not match other records. Investigators and historians treat him as an important *informant*, a person who gives inside information to the authorities. His account still has to be checked against other evidence.

lessons.title: Tongs: Brotherhood and Mutual Aid
lessons.mainIdea: Chinese American tongs began mostly as mutual-aid brotherhoods; some also ran gambling, but most members were ordinary workers and merchants.
reading: In 1882, Congress passed the *Chinese Exclusion Act*. It barred most new Chinese workers from entering the United States. Chinese immigrants already here faced unfair laws and violence. Many could not turn to the courts or city hall for help. So they built their own associations, based on family names, home districts and brotherhood.

A *tong* is one kind of these associations. The word means a hall or meeting place. Tongs offered *mutual aid*: members helped each other find jobs, housing and lawyers. They lent money and settled arguments. Other Chinese associations, based on home districts, helped send the dead home for burial in China. For many men far from their families, the tong was a second home.

Some tongs also ran gambling halls and other illegal businesses. Rival tongs sometimes fought what newspapers called tong wars. In New York in the early 1900s, the Hip Sing and On Leong tongs fought around Doyers Street in Chinatown. These fights were real. But they were not the whole story, and most tong members never took part in them.

Chicago shows both sides. In 1926 and 1927 the On Leong Merchants Association built a grand building at 2216 South Wentworth Avenue, a meeting place for the Chinatown community. In 1988 FBI agents and Chicago police raided it and found an illegal casino, and the government seized the building. A church bought it in 1993, and in 1994 it became the Pui Tak Center, a community center. It is a Chicago Landmark.

lessons.title: Triads: Legend and Record
lessons.mainIdea: Triads descend from the Heaven and Earth Society, founded around 1761 as a mutual-aid brotherhood, though its legend places its start a century earlier.
reading: Triad members tell a founding *legend*. In the 1670s, it says, loyal monks of the Shaolin monastery were betrayed by the emperor. Five survivors swore to overthrow the Qing dynasty and bring back the old Ming rulers. The story appears in the society's own ritual books. It gave members a heroic past and a cause.

Records tell a different story. Qing government files, studied by the historians Dian Murray and Qin Baoqi in 1994, show that the *Heaven and Earth Society*, called the Tiandihui, began around 1761 or 1762 in Zhangpu county, Fujian. It started as a brotherhood for poor men who moved around looking for work and needed each other's help. Its anti-Qing slogans grew later.

The government learned much about the society after a crackdown in Taiwan in 1786 and a rising there in 1787 and 1788. Arrested members described it under questioning. Over time the society split into many groups, known together as the Hongmen. Some became political. In 1904 in Honolulu, the revolutionary Sun Yat-sen joined the Chee Kung Tong, a Hongmen group, to win support from Chinese people abroad.

The English word *triad* came later, from the society's symbol joining heaven, earth and humankind. Some later triad groups, especially in Hong Kong, became criminal. Scholars say modern triads descend from the old society but are not the same thing. As with the Mafia, historians separate the legend from the records, and old roots from later crimes.

chapters.title: Breaking the Silence
chapters.bigQuestion: What does it take for a law, a court and a whole city to break a rule of silence that lasted more than a century?

story.title: Stickers in the Night
story.kicker: On one June night in 2004, a few young people in Palermo quietly change what their city talks about.
paragraphs: It is the night of 28 June 2004 in Palermo, the capital of Sicily. A small group of young friends walks through the old city center. They carry small stickers with a black border, like the notices Italians post to announce a death. They press them onto walls, poles and doors. By morning, stickers are all over the center of the city.

Each sticker carries one sentence in Italian: 'Un intero popolo che paga il pizzo è un popolo senza dignità.' In English it means that a whole people who pays the pizzo is a people without dignity. The pizzo is protection money. For generations, many Palermo shopkeepers had paid it to the Mafia, quietly, because refusing felt too dangerous.

The stickers did not name anyone. They did not threaten anyone. They simply said out loud what many people knew and few people said. Soon the stickers were in the news. Shopkeepers, customers and students began to talk about the pizzo in public, and some shopkeepers later joined the young people's campaign.

This was not the first time Palermo had broken its silence. Twelve years earlier, in 1992, two judges named Giovanni Falcone and Paolo Borsellino had been murdered by the Mafia. Their work, and their deaths, had changed what many Sicilians believed was possible. This chapter tells how new laws, brave witnesses and ordinary people fought back.
story.think: Why do you think the young people chose a sticker with a black border instead of a speech or a march? What can a small, quiet act do?

sections.title: A New Law for an Old Problem

lessons.title: The RICO Act
lessons.mainIdea: RICO, signed on 15 October 1970, lets prosecutors charge people for running or taking part in a criminal organization, not just for single crimes.
reading: For decades, American prosecutors faced a problem. They could charge a gunman for a shooting or a collector for a threat. But the bosses who gave the orders rarely touched a gun or wrote anything down. A family could lose members to prison and keep running. The organization itself stayed out of reach.

On 15 October 1970, President Richard Nixon signed the Organized Crime Control Act. Title IX of that law is the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, known as *RICO*. Its main author was G. Robert Blakey, a lawyer who worked for the Senate and later taught law.

RICO made it a crime to run or take part in an *enterprise*, meaning any group of people working together, through a *pattern of racketeering activity*. A pattern means at least two related crimes of certain listed kinds within ten years. The list includes murder, extortion, bribery and illegal gambling.

This mattered for three reasons. Prosecutors could now try a boss for the whole pattern of an organization's crimes. They could put many members on trial together and show a jury the big picture. And the government could take away property and money gained through the enterprise, a step called *forfeiture*.

lessons.title: RICO in the Courtroom
lessons.mainIdea: From the 1980s, prosecutors used RICO to try whole crime families at once, and even the leaders of several families together.
reading: At first RICO was used slowly. Prosecutors and judges were still learning how it worked. In the 1980s that changed. Federal prosecutors began building large cases that treated a crime family as the enterprise. Court-approved *wiretaps* and hidden microphones gave them the bosses' own words.

In New York, prosecutors went further. In what became known as the *Commission case*, begun in 1985, they charged leaders from several of the city's families together. They argued that the Commission, the council of bosses, was itself a criminal enterprise. In 1986 a jury convicted the defendants, and long prison sentences followed.

RICO also has a civil side. People harmed by an enterprise can sue for *damages*, money to make up for harm, and the law allows three times the loss. The government has also used civil RICO to take control of labor unions that crime families had captured, and to appoint monitors to clean them up.

Critics say RICO is very broad. Because an enterprise can be almost any group, prosecutors have used it against businesses, street gangs and public officials, not only the Mafia. Defenders say the breadth is the point: organized crime changes shape, so the law has to fit many shapes. You can weigh both sides.

lessons.title: The Anti-Mafia Pool
lessons.mainIdea: Palermo magistrates formed a pool that shared every file, so the Mafia could not stop an investigation by killing one judge.
reading: In Italy, an *investigating magistrate* is a judge who gathers evidence and builds a case before trial. In Palermo in the early 1980s, that job was deadly. Magistrates who looked into the Mafia often worked alone, and some were killed. When one died, much of his knowledge died with him.

Rocco Chinnici, the head of Palermo's investigating office, had an idea. What if a small team shared every file? Then no single death could stop the work. On 29 July 1983, Chinnici was killed by a car bomb. His *successor*, Antonino Caponnetto, made the idea real. The team became known as the *anti-Mafia pool*.

The pool included Giovanni Falcone and Paolo Borsellino, two magistrates who had grown up in Palermo and had known each other since childhood. Falcone was known for following the money: bank records and cash that tied crimes together. The pool's members lived with armed guards and could rarely go anywhere freely.

The pool's method was patient. Link each crime to others. Link each person to a family. Then show that the families belonged to one organization. That last step was the hardest. It needed someone from the inside who knew how the whole structure worked.

lessons.title: Buscetta Breaks the Silence
lessons.mainIdea: From 1984, longtime Mafia member Tommaso Buscetta told Falcone how Cosa Nostra was organized, breaking omertà from the inside.
reading: Tommaso Buscetta had been a member of Cosa Nostra for decades. In the early 1980s a violent war broke out inside the Mafia. A *faction* from the town of Corleone killed many rivals, and several of Buscetta's relatives were among the dead. Buscetta was living in Brazil when police there arrested him in October 1983.

In 1984 he was sent back to Italy. From July 1984, he answered Giovanni Falcone's questions in Rome. The sessions lasted months. Falcone wrote Buscetta's words down by hand, filling hundreds of pages. Buscetta became Italy's most famous *pentito*, a word for a Mafia member who turns and cooperates with justice.

Buscetta explained the structure. Each family ruled a territory. Families were grouped into districts. Above them sat a ruling body called the *Commission*. He described rules, ranks and the oath of loyalty. His picture fit what Sangiorgi had described around Palermo more than eighty years before.

Why did he talk? Buscetta said the Mafia had betrayed its own old rules. Critics noted that he also had reason to want revenge on the men who killed his relatives. Both can be true. Falcone's rule was to check everything. A pentito's words mattered most when other evidence, such as bank records or other witnesses, backed them up.

lessons.title: The Bunker Courtroom
lessons.mainIdea: The Maxi Trial opened on 10 February 1986 in a specially built, attack-resistant courtroom in Palermo, with 475 people charged.
reading: Using Buscetta's evidence and years of their own work, the pool wrote the charges. In Italy this document was called an ordinanza-sentenza, a kind of *indictment* in which the investigating judges lay out the case for trial. It was filed on 8 November 1985. It filled about 40 volumes and roughly 8,000 pages.

The case charged 475 people. No ordinary courtroom could hold that many *defendants*. So the state built a new hall beside the Ucciardone prison in Palermo. It was called the *bunker courtroom* because it was built to resist attack. Defendants sat in barred cells along the sides of the hall.

The Maxi Trial opened on 10 February 1986. The word maxi means very large. It was one of the largest criminal trials ever held. Reporters came from around the world. Many people in Palermo had never before seen Mafia members named, one by one, in a public court.

The trial tested the pool's main idea. Could a court accept that hundreds of people belonged to one organization, Cosa Nostra, with a Commission at the top? If so, leaders could be held responsible for crimes their organization carried out. That idea later came to be called the Buscetta theorem.

lessons.title: The Verdict and the Appeal
lessons.mainIdea: On 16 December 1987 the court convicted more than 330 people, and in January 1992 Italy's highest court upheld the verdict.
reading: The trial lasted almost two years. On 16 December 1987 the court gave its *verdict*. Most Italian sources report that 346 people were convicted and 114 were acquitted. Some sources give slightly lower counts, between 338 and 344, so it is safest to say more than 330. Nineteen people received life sentences.

In Italy a verdict is not final until it passes through *appeal*, when a higher court reviews the case. The top court for criminal cases is the *Court of Cassation* in Rome. On 30 January 1992, it upheld the Maxi Trial's verdict. It also accepted the key finding: Cosa Nostra is one organization, led by a Commission.

This was a turning point. Italy's highest court had confirmed what Sangiorgi, Buscetta and the pool had described. Mafia leaders could now be held responsible as leaders. Life sentences for bosses were final. The silence that had protected the organization for more than a century had been broken in law.

Why do the conviction counts differ? Large trials have many defendants whose cases change. Some defendants die, some are tried separately, and some charges are combined. Different writers counted at different moments. Good historians report the range and say where each number comes from.

lessons.title: Capaci and Via D'Amelio
lessons.mainIdea: In 1992 the Mafia murdered Giovanni Falcone and Paolo Borsellino, along with Francesca Morvillo and eight police officers who protected them.
reading: The Maxi Trial made the magistrates targets. On 23 May 1992, a bomb exploded under the highway near Capaci as Falcone's cars drove from the Palermo airport toward the city. Falcone was killed. So were his wife, Francesca Morvillo, who was also a *magistrate*, and three police officers of his *escort*: Antonio Montinaro, Rocco Dicillo and Vito Schifani.

Fifty-seven days later came a second attack. On 19 July 1992, a car bomb exploded on Via D'Amelio in Palermo. Borsellino had come there to visit his mother. Borsellino was killed with five officers of his escort: Emanuela Loi, Agostino Catalano, Vincenzo Li Muli, Walter Eddie Cosina and Claudio Traina.

Italian courts later convicted Salvatore Riina, the head of the Corleone faction, and many others for these attacks. Some questions are still being examined in court, including whether people outside the Mafia played a role. Investigators also learned that one early witness in the Via D'Amelio case had given false *testimony*, which led to new trials years later.

These were not only attacks on two men. They were attacks on the idea that the law could win. The Mafia wanted to frighten judges, police and witnesses back into silence. We remember the escort officers by name too, because they chose to stand beside the judges, knowing the danger.

words.d: in Italy, a judge or a public prosecutor
a team of officers who travel with a person to protect them
what a witness says in court under oath

lessons.title: Palermo Speaks Up
lessons.mainIdea: After 1992, ordinary people broke public silence with sheets on balconies, a priest's work with children and a national network called Libera.
reading: In the weeks after the 1992 killings, many families in Palermo hung white bedsheets from their balconies. Some had words painted on them against the Mafia. It was a simple act. But many people were showing their neighbors, in public, which side they were on.

In the Brancaccio neighborhood, a parish priest named Pino Puglisi opened a center so children would have somewhere to go besides the street. He taught that young people could choose a different life. On 15 September 1993, his 56th birthday, he was murdered. In 2013 the Catholic Church *beatified* him, a step toward naming him a saint.

In 1995 a priest from Turin, Luigi Ciotti, founded *Libera*, a national network of anti-Mafia groups. Libera works with families of victims and with schools. It helps turn land and buildings taken from Mafia bosses into farms, cooperatives and community spaces. The idea is that stolen wealth should come back to the public.

An *anti-Mafia movement* is not one group. It is many people acting in many ways: teachers, priests, shopkeepers, students, reporters and families of victims. A saying often credited to Falcone puts the hope plainly. The Mafia is a human thing, it says, and like every human thing it had a beginning and will have an end.

words.d: declared blessed by the Catholic Church, a step toward being named a saint
an Italian network of anti-Mafia groups founded in 1995 by Luigi Ciotti
the many people and groups who work in different ways to resist the Mafia

lessons.title: Addiopizzo: Goodbye, Pizzo
lessons.mainIdea: Addiopizzo, begun by young people in 2004, turned refusing protection money into something shops and customers could do together.
reading: The *pizzo* is protection money paid to the Mafia. It is the same business Franchetti described in 1877, in modern form. A shop pays regularly, often every month. In return, nothing bad happens to it. For a single shopkeeper, refusing alone could feel impossible. The collector might come back with threats, or worse.

The young people who put up the stickers in June 2004 understood this. So they looked for a way to make refusing a shared act. Their movement, called *Addiopizzo*, meaning goodbye pizzo, invited shops to say publicly that they did not pay. Shopkeepers joined over time.

Addiopizzo then asked customers to take a side too. People could sign a pledge to shop at stores that refused to pay. A published list of pizzo-free businesses helped them find those stores. This idea is called *critical consumption*: choosing where to spend money so that it supports honest businesses.

The strategy changed the math. One shop refusing alone is a target. Many shops refusing together, with customers behind them and police ready to act, are much harder to punish. Addiopizzo also supports shopkeepers who report extortion, helping them through the police and court process.

words.d: protection money that the Mafia demands from shops and businesses

sections.title: Chicago, Witnesses and the Real Cost

lessons.title: Operation Family Secrets
lessons.mainIdea: In 2007 a federal jury in Chicago convicted leaders of the Outfit in a RICO case that covered 18 old murders.
reading: For decades, murders linked to Chicago's Outfit went unsolved. Families of victims waited without answers. In the early 2000s, federal agents and prosecutors in Chicago built a case they named *Operation Family Secrets*. They used RICO to charge Outfit members with a long-running *racketeering* conspiracy that included 18 murders from past decades.

A key witness came from inside one family. Frank Calabrese Jr. agreed to wear a hidden recording device, called a *wire*, while talking with his own father, Frank Calabrese Sr. Later he testified in court against him. It was one of the hardest choices a witness can make.

On 10 September 2007 the jury found all five defendants guilty of racketeering conspiracy. On 27 September it found that three of them, Frank Calabrese Sr., Joseph Lombardo and James Marcello, were responsible for murders. For many victims' families, the trial was the first time the full story was told in public.

The case shows RICO doing what its authors hoped. Old murders that could not easily be tried one at a time became part of one pattern. It also shows omertà breaking in a very personal way: a son chose his conscience over his father's code of silence.

words.d: a federal RICO case in Chicago, tried in 2007, against leaders of the Outfit
making money through repeated crimes such as extortion, bribery or illegal gambling
a hidden recording device worn by a person to record conversations

lessons.title: Can an Insider Be Trusted?
lessons.mainIdea: Witnesses from inside a crime group are powerful but risky, so courts need corroboration from other evidence.
reading: Almost every big case in this unit depended on someone from the inside: Valachi, Buscetta, Frank Calabrese Jr. Only insiders know how a secret group really works. But insiders may have reasons to bend the truth. They may want a lighter sentence, protection, money or revenge.

Courts deal with this through *corroboration*: evidence from another source that supports what a witness says. Falcone checked Buscetta's words against bank records and other witnesses. In Chicago, the recordings Frank Calabrese Jr. made let the jury hear a defendant's own voice.

When checking fails, justice can fail too. In the Via D'Amelio case, a man named Vincenzo Scarantino confessed and named others. Years later, courts found that his story was false, and convictions based on it were overturned. Italian courts are still examining how that mistake happened.

Governments also protect witnesses who tell the truth. The United States set up a federal *witness protection* program under the same 1970 Organized Crime Control Act that contained RICO. It can give a witness a new name and a new home. Italy built its own system to protect collaborators of justice.

words.d: evidence from another source that supports what a witness says
a government program that keeps witnesses safe, sometimes with a new name and home
a person who belongs to a group and knows its secrets

lessons.title: The Real Cost
lessons.mainIdea: Organized crime takes money, safety and trust from ordinary people, and those who resist it have paid the highest price.
reading: Films often show crime families as clever, stylish and loyal. The record tells a different story. Think of a family that runs a bakery. Every month, part of what they earn goes to the pizzo. That money comes out of wages, prices and savings. Customers pay more. Honest competitors can be pushed out.

The costs spread wider. When officials are bribed, people stop trusting police and courts. When *public works* such as roads and schools are rigged, they cost more and may be built worse. When witnesses are killed, like William Drury in Chicago in 1950, others learn to stay silent. Fear becomes a kind of tax too.

Whole communities have paid in another way: *prejudice*. Italian Americans and Chinese Americans were often blamed as groups for the crimes of a few. In 1891 that prejudice led to a mob killing in New Orleans. Most victims of the Black Hand and of the pizzo came from the same communities the criminals claimed to belong to.

The heaviest price was paid by those who resisted: Emanuele Notarbartolo, Rocco Chinnici, Giovanni Falcone, Francesca Morvillo, Paolo Borsellino, their escort officers and Father Puglisi. Their stories show what this unit has traced from 1876 to today. Silence protected the Mafia. Speaking up, together and with protection, is what weakened it.
